documents.title: Gynecology Consultation
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
Gynecology consultation. Date of visit 12/24/2019.

Dear Doctor,

I saw Ms. Thayer, 22, at your request for genital lesions she has had for about two months. They are not painful, but she is bothered by how they look. She has had no fevers, urinary symptoms or vaginal discharge.

Medical history unremarkable. No surgeries. No medications. No known drug allergies. Family history of hypothyroidism in her mother and hypertension in her father; a sibling is well. She reports more than one sexual partner and does not use condoms every time.

On exam there are several cauliflower-like growths, 1 to 2 cm each, on the vulva. No lymphadenopathy. Remainder of the exam is normal.

We shave biopsied one lesion in the office. Pathology returned on 12/27 showing squamous cell papillomatosis without dysplasia, consistent with condyloma acuminatum. I called her with the result and sent imiquimod 5% cream to use at bedtime three nights a week, washed off in the morning, for up to 16 weeks. I explained that local redness and irritation are expected and that she can pause for a few days if it becomes too sore. She should come back if the lesions are not clearly better in two to three months.

Thank you for the referral.

Gynecology

DERMATOLOGY NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 04/03/2020
Referred by: primary care

Reason for consult: several small skin lesions over the past two weeks.

History: 23-year-old woman seen by gynecology in late December for vulvar condylomata. About two weeks ago she noticed one papule on the inner thigh and ignored it; a few more have come up in the same area since. They are not painful or itchy and have not drained. No prior skin problems like this. No fevers or other systemic symptoms. She had one day of diarrhea about three weeks ago that settled without treatment.

Problems: condylomata acuminata.
Medications: imiquimod 5% cream (vulva).
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: mother hypothyroidism, father hypertension, sibling healthy.
Social: marketing consultant. Sexually active, new partner.

Vitals within normal limits.

Exam: inner thigh and adjacent skin with several small, firm, skin-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Remainder of the examined skin unremarkable.

Assessment: molluscum contagiosum.

Plan: discussed that this is a self-limited viral infection that usually clears on its own over months. She prefers to let it run its course rather than have the lesions treated. Avoid shaving or picking the area; can spread by skin contact including with partners. Return if they spread widely or become inflamed.

Dermatology

documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Dermatology clinic note. Visit date 06/22/2020.

Dear Doctor,

Ms. Thayer returns, previously seen by gynecology in December and by our clinic in April. For roughly three weeks she has had vulvar itching with mild discomfort and has noticed growths near the vaginal opening that are slowly getting larger. LMP 10 days ago, normal. She has had two male partners in the past year and does not always use condoms. No abnormal discharge, fevers or dysuria.

Problem list: condylomata acuminata; molluscum contagiosum.
Medications: none current (imiquimod course completed).
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: along the labia minora and posterior introitus there are multiple soft, exophytic, pink papules with a verrucous surface, 5 to 10 mm. Vagina and cervix look normal. No bleeding, no discharge.

Assessment: recurrent condylomata acuminata.

Procedure: after verbal consent, cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, two freeze-thaw cycles to each visible lesion. Tolerated well. Expect blistering and soreness for several days; sitz baths and plain petrolatum for comfort.

We will see her back as needed. Condoms reduce but do not eliminate transmission; HPV vaccination remains reasonable at her age.

Dermatology

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN NOTE
Arrival 12/24/2023 14:05. Sent in by her PCP.

CC: joint pain and fever x3 days.

HPI: 26 y/o F with prior recurrent condylomata and remote molluscum, here with three days of fevers and progressively worse joint pain. Right knee and left wrist painful and swollen, as are several fingers; trouble gripping things and walking. Since yesterday a painful rash of red bumps and tiny blisters on both forearms and ankles. A week of on-and-off lower abdominal discomfort with vaginal spotting, plus a yellowish discharge, no itching, no odor. LMP 2 weeks ago. Sexually active with multiple partners, barrier protection inconsistent. Denies IV drug use.

PMH: condylomata acuminata, molluscum contagiosum. PSH none. Meds none. NKDA. FH: mother hypothyroidism, father HTN, sibling healthy. SH: never smoker, social alcohol.

Exam: T 38.9, HR 112, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA. Febrile, uncomfortable-appearing. Left wrist and right knee swollen with reduced range of motion. Tender along the flexor tendon sheaths of the left hand. Scattered pustules on erythematous bases over the distal arms and legs. Heart tachycardic, regular; lungs clear; abdomen soft. Speculum: cervix friable with mucopurulent discharge. No cervical motion tenderness. No adnexal tenderness.

ED course: CBC, CMP, CRP, ESR, urine hCG, blood cultures x2. Cervical swab for GC/CT NAAT. Right knee arthrocentesis under sterile technique, fluid sent for cell count, crystals, Gram stain and culture. HIV and RPR sent. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV given. Repeat T 38.4, HR 104.

WBC 13.4 (82% PMN). CRP 96. ESR 48. CMP unremarkable. hCG negative. Synovial fluid inflammatory; Gram stain without organisms.

Assessment: suspected disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis, plus cervicitis.
Disposition: admitted to medicine for IV ceftriaxone.

Addendum 12/25: cervical NAAT positive for N. gonorrhoeae, negative for C. trachomatis. Diagnosis confirmed.

medications.sig: 1 g IV every 24 hours for 7 days total

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 12/24/2023. Discharged 12/30/2023.
Admitting/discharge diagnosis: disseminated gonococcal infection (arthritis-dermatitis), with gonococcal cervicitis.

Hospital course: 26 year old woman admitted from the ED with fever, polyarthritis of the right knee and left wrist, left hand flexor tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions of the distal extremities. Cervical NAAT returned positive for gonorrhea, negative for chlamydia. Blood cultures x2 no growth at 5 days. Right knee synovial fluid: WBC 42,000, 88% neutrophils, no crystals, Gram stain negative, culture no growth. HIV and RPR nonreactive.

Treated with ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours, 7 doses, completed before discharge. Fevers resolved by hospital day 2. Joint swelling and skin lesions improved steadily. Day 4 labs: WBC 9.1, CRP 31 (from 96).

Partner notification and testing discussed; she has the information to share with recent partners. Abstain from sex until partners are treated and her symptoms are gone. Repeat GC/CT testing in about 3 months.

Discharge medications: none.
Allergies: NKDA.
Condition at discharge: afebrile, ambulating, improved.
Follow-up: PCP within one week.

documents.body: Transitional care call. Discharged 12/30 after 7 days of IV ceftriaxone for disseminated gonococcal infection. Home, no fevers, walking fine, knee and wrist better each day. No discharge meds to reconcile, takes nothing at home. Confirmed appointment Thursday 1/4 at 11. Knows to call for fever or a hot, swollen joint.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 5 days after discharge. Admitted 12/24-12/30 for disseminated gonococcal infection: fever, right knee and left wrist arthritis, left hand flexor tenosynovitis, pustular rash, cervicitis. Cervical NAAT positive for GC, CT negative. Blood and knee fluid cultures negative. 7 days of IV ceftriaxone completed inpatient. Discharge summary and ED record reviewed.

Since home: no fevers. Knee and wrist much better, still a little stiff in the mornings. Spots on the arms and ankles scabbing over. No discharge or spotting now. Hasn't been sexually active since. Has told recent partners to get tested.

Meds none. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile, vitals normal. Right knee with mild residual swelling, no warmth, flexes nearly fully. Left wrist mildly puffy, near-full range of motion, grip ok. Flexor tendons of the left hand not tender. Skin: crusted, fading lesions on the forearms and ankles.

A/P:
1. DGI, improving after a full course of ceftriaxone. CBC and CRP today to make sure they're trending down. Recheck in 2-3 weeks.
2. Retest GC/CT around late March.
3. Condoms every time going forward; we talked about partner testing and how she'd know if it came back.

Date of service: 12/19/2024
Copy to primary care.

CC: three days of fever, malaise, painful urination and worsening genital pain.

HPI: 27 y/o seen here previously for condylomata, with a disseminated gonococcal infection last December. Three days of feeling feverish and achy with chills, burning on urination, and genital tenderness that keeps increasing; sitting is difficult because of vulvar pain. No abnormal discharge and no pelvic pain.

Problem list: condylomata acuminata; molluscum contagiosum; disseminated gonococcal infection (treated 12/2023).
Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother hypothyroidism; father hypertension; sibling healthy.
SH: three male partners in the last six months. Condoms inconsistently. No contraception.

Vitals: T 37.0 C, P 80, BP 110/70.

Pelvic exam: multiple vesicles and shallow ulcers over the labia minora and majora, exquisitely tender to light touch. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes enlarged, firm and tender.

Assessment: primary genital herpes simplex infection.

Plan:
- Lesion swab for HSV PCR; GC/CT NAAT.
- Valacyclovir 1 g twice daily for 10 days.
- Sitz baths; urinating in a warm bath or with a peri bottle helps the burning.
- Abstain until lesions are fully healed.

Addendum 12/21: PCR positive for HSV-2, negative for HSV-1. GC/CT negative. Patient informed by phone; discussed lifelong latency, possible recurrences, asymptomatic shedding and disclosure to partners.

documents.title: Telehealth Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, patient at home.

First-episode genital herpes diagnosed by gyn 12/19, PCR HSV-2. Finished 10 days of valacyclovir. Sores healed, no fever, urinating comfortably.

Mostly wanted to talk. Covered: HSV-2 stays in the body and may or may not recur, first episodes are usually the worst; it can be passed on without symptoms; condoms lower risk; telling partners before sex. Answered her questions about dating. She seemed relieved.

A/P: Primary genital HSV-2, episode resolved. Message at the first tingling or sores so we can arrange to be seen. Annual physical in September.

documents.body:
Gynecology office visit, 01/05/2026. cc: PCP.

Reason for visit: painful genital sores and burning with urination for 4 days.

History: 28 year old with prior condylomata, DGI (2023), and a primary genital herpes episode in December 2024 (HSV-2 by PCR). This started with genital burning and tingling, then small fluid-filled blisters that opened into shallow, tender sores. Low-grade fevers, fatigue, sore lumps in the groin.

Problems: condylomata acuminata; molluscum contagiosum; disseminated gonococcal infection; genital herpes.
Medications: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Social: one new partner; condoms not consistently.

Exam: multiple shallow, red, clean-based ulcers on the vulva and outer labia. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Assessment: recurrent genital herpes.

Plan: swab of one ulcer for HSV PCR. Valacyclovir 1 g daily for 5 days. Comfort measures as before. Avoid sexual contact until healed and let her partner know.

Addendum 01/07: PCR positive for HSV-2.
